Both start the same way, with a jealous husband and no witness. A hunch isn't a fact, and I once swore somebody swiped my last cookie when it was in my apron pocket the whole time.

I get why this one feels shaky, but the text says otherwise. The LORD spells out a second case: a feeling of jealousy comes over the husband and he suspects his wife “…even though she has not defiled herself…” (Numbers 5:14). So the law covers the wife who has gone astray and the wife who hasn't. The summary at the end says it again, naming a husband who suspects his wife (Numbers 5:30). Both cases follow the same steps.

That's it, baker. The text says the husband is to bring his wife to the priest. The priest then has her stand before the LORD, so the whole thing happens in front of Him and not in the husband's living room. Notice nobody is told to take it to a neighbor or settle it with a shouting match.

Elders do show up in Israel (Exodus 3:16), but not in this law. Numbers 5:15 says the husband brings his wife to the priest. The priest is the one who then has her stand before the LORD and handles every step after that. So the elders can stay home for this one.

Judges are a fair guess, friend, since that's who we picture when something needs settling. But this passage never sends the husband to one. He is to bring his wife to the priest (Numbers 5:15). The priest has the woman stand before the LORD and carries out the law from start to finish.

Barley flour, yes. The text says a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. And no oil and no frankincense on top, which is a plain offering, like a cookie with no sprinkles. I love sprinkles, but this is the instruction the LORD gave.
Wheat flour is what I'd grab first, friend. It's what my kitchen runs on. But Numbers 5:15 names barley flour, a tenth of an ephah of it. The text lists no oil and no frankincense with it either.

Roasted grain sounds like a nice crunchy snack, but it's not what the text says. The offering is a tenth of an ephah of barley flour. It's flour, not roasted grain. The text also says he is not to pour oil over it or put frankincense on it.

I see why you'd go there, since sacrifices come up a lot in the Bible. But this passage doesn't put blood in the jar. The text doesn't mention a covering here. It says the priest lets down her hair after she stands before the LORD, and then he places the grain offering in her hands (Numbers 5:18). explanations.answer: May she be immune to it
explanations.explanation: That's the one. If no other man has slept with her, the priest says, “…may you be immune to this bitter water that brings a curse.” Verse 28 backs it up: if she is clean, she will be unaffected and able to conceive children. Immune, baker. That's the word on the page.

explanations.answer: May she be healed by it
explanations.explanation: Healed is a kind word, but the priest doesn't say it. The text has him say, “…may you be immune to this bitter water that brings a curse.” Immune means it doesn't touch her. Later the text says that if she is clean she will be unaffected (Numbers 5:28).

explanations.answer: May she be forgiven by it
explanations.explanation: Forgiveness is a big theme in the Bible, friend, but it isn't what the priest says here. The oath says, “…may you be immune to this bitter water that brings a curse.” That's about the water not affecting her, if she hasn't gone astray. The text puts it in those words, so I'll leave them as they are.

Close, but check who's doing the cursing. The priest says, “then may the LORD make you an attested curse among your people…” (Numbers 5:21). So it's the LORD in that line, not the husband. This is a heavy part of the law, and it's worth reading each word carefully.

Right, baker. The priest says the words “then may the LORD make you an attested curse among your people by making your thigh shrivel and your belly swell.” The husband isn't the one named in that line. It's the LORD. This is one of the heavy parts, so it matters to get the words right.
Yes, “Amen, Amen.” That's the woman's whole answer after the priest speaks the curse over her (Numbers 5:22). One word, said twice. Sometimes the shortest line in the passage is the one that counts.

That would be a fine thing to say, friend, but it isn't in this passage. After the priest speaks the curse, the woman says, “Amen, Amen.” That's all the text gives her to say there. I'd rather give you the exact words than add some of my own.

I can see why you'd reach for that one, but the text doesn't give her those words. After the priest speaks the curse, she says, “Amen, Amen” (Numbers 5:22). That's her whole reply at that moment. I won't add lines the Bible didn't write.

explanations.answer: Washes them off into the bitter water
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's what the text says. The priest writes the curses on a scroll and washes them off into the bitter water (Numbers 5:23). After that, he burns a handful of the grain offering on the altar, and then he has the woman drink the water (Numbers 5:26). I think this is a heavy part of the passage, so it's worth reading slowly.

explanations.answer: Burns the scroll on the altar
explanations.explanation: Burning at the altar does show up in this passage, but it's the grain offering. The priest burns a handful of it as a memorial portion (Numbers 5:26). For the curses, the text says he writes them on a scroll and washes them off into the bitter water (Numbers 5:23). It doesn't mention the scroll going to the altar.

explanations.answer: Reads them aloud to the camp
explanations.explanation: A big public reading would be a whole different scene, friend. The text doesn't have the priest do that with this scroll. He writes the curses and washes them off into the bitter water (Numbers 5:23). From there the water is what the woman is to drink.

Almost, but the word "whole" is the catch. The text says the priest takes a handful of the grain offering as a memorial portion and burns that on the altar (Numbers 5:26). A handful, not the entire offering. It's a tiny detail, and it's easy to slide past.

Right, baker. The priest takes a handful of the grain offering as a memorial portion and burns it on the altar (Numbers 5:26). He doesn't burn the whole offering, just the handful. Good eye on a small detail.

Yes, that's what verse 28 says. If the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, she will be unaffected and able to conceive children. It's the other side of the curse we just heard. The text gives both outcomes, and this one is the clean one.

Not quite, friend. Verse 28 says if the woman has not defiled herself and is clean, she will be unaffected and able to conceive children. That's the other side of the curse the priest spoke over her. So the answer on this one is True.

Priest it is. Verse 30 says the woman stands before the LORD, and the priest is to apply to her this entire law. He's the one all the way through, from bringing her forward to burning the handful on the altar. One person running the whole show is easier than three cooks and one oven.

The husband is in this law, but he isn't the one who applies it. His part is bringing his wife and the offering to the priest (Numbers 5:15). Verse 30 says the priest is to apply to her this entire law. So the priest is the one doing the work.
Judge is a natural guess, friend. But there's no judge anywhere in Numbers 5:11-31. Verse 30 says the priest is to apply to her this entire law. That's the one name the text gives for the job.

explanations.answer: He will be free from guilt
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's how the law closes about the husband. Verse 31 says he will be free from guilt. The next part of the verse is about the woman, and it's a heavy line. I think this is a part of the passage that's meant to be read slowly.

explanations.answer: He will bring a ram of atonement
explanations.explanation: A ram of atonement does appear a few verses earlier, in a different law (Numbers 5:8). This law ends with a different line about the husband. Verse 31 says he will be free from guilt. He isn't told to bring anything else here. Two laws in the same chapter, so I get the mix-up.

explanations.explanation: Repaying a fifth more is a real thing in Numbers 5:7, just a few verses earlier, and it's for a different matter. This law ends with a different line about the husband. Verse 31 says he will be free from guilt. Two laws in the same chapter, so I get the mix-up.
